## Overview

QTSim follows one population. The categorical layer of QTLSim places populations side by
side as demes, with the monoidal product `⊗` of the life cycle, and couples them with a
migration step, `migrate(k)`
([One life cycle, two backends](../07_one_life_cycle_two_backends/07_one_life_cycle_two_backends.qmd)).
This vignette shows how to build and run such metapopulations, explains what the
kernel's migration does, and checks the simulated differentiation among neutral demes
against population-genetic theory: Wright's island model [@Wright1931], its exact
finite-island form [@Takahata1983], the stepping-stone ring [@KimuraWeiss1964;
@Slatkin1991], and the neutral theory of quantitative variation in a subdivided
population [@Lande1992; @Whitlock1999]. It ends with demes adapted to optima of their
own, whose differentiation in the trait exceeds the neutral expectation.

## Setup

```{julia}
using QTLSim
import Catlab                       # loads the categorical layer
using Catlab: ⋅, ⊗
using CairoMakie, Printf, Random, Statistics
using Distributions: Normal, cdf
CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png")
L = lifecycle(); g = L.generation   # QTSim's generation, Zygotes → Zygotes
```

## Building a metapopulation

A metapopulation needs two things: populations, one per deme, and a life cycle on all of
them. `p ⊗ demes(k)` makes `k` demes with the parameters `p`. The life cycle
`g ⊗ g ⊗ g ⊗ g` runs QTSim's generation in each of four demes, and composing it with
`L.migrate(4)` adds a migration step after the generation:

```{julia}
p = Params(PopSize = 200, NoQTL = 10, Ploidy = 2, NoGenerations = 500, PhenotypeVar = 1.0,
           Heritability = 0.5, MutationScalar = 0.01, MutationRatePerGamete = 0.01, Drift = true)
cycle = g ⊗ g ⊗ g ⊗ g ⋅ L.migrate(4)
```

`run_composed` runs it. `migration_rate` is the probability that an individual starts an
exchange with an individual of another deme, chosen at random among the other three. The
records have one row per deme and generation, with the deme in the column `deme`. With
`Drift = true` every individual has fitness one, so the demes drift apart, and migration
holds them together:

```{julia}
o = run_composed(p ⊗ demes(4), Xoshiro(1); cycle, migration_rate = 0.01)
last_gen = o.gen .== 499
for d in 1:4
    i = findfirst(last_gen .& (o.deme .== d))
    @printf("deme %d, generation 499: mean phenotype %6.3f, genetic variance %.4f, size %d\n",
            d, o.pheno_mean[i], o.geno_var[i], o.popsize[i])
end
```

A scalar rate is the island model. For other graphs, `migration_rate` takes a matrix
whose entry `[a, b]` is the probability that an individual of deme `a` starts an
exchange with a random individual of deme `b`: `island_migration(k, r)` is the island
model as a matrix, and `stepping_stone(k, r)` sends half of `r` to each neighbour on a
ring (or, with `circular = false`, a line).

```{julia}
stepping_stone(6, 0.02)
```

```{julia}
o_ring = run_composed(p ⊗ demes(6), Xoshiro(2); cycle = foldl(⊗, fill(g, 6)) ⋅ L.migrate(6),
                      migration_rate = stepping_stone(6, 0.02))
size(o_ring.gen)
```

Demes can have parameters of their own in two ways. A vector of `Params`,
`[p1, …, pk] ⊗ demes(k)`, gives each deme its own constants: here four demes of
different sizes. Because migration exchanges individuals, each keeps its size exactly:

```{julia}
sizes = [50, 100, 200, 400]
o_sizes = run_composed([Params(p; PopSize = n) for n in sizes] ⊗ demes(4), Xoshiro(3); cycle,
                       migration_rate = 0.05)
[extrema(o_sizes.popsize[o_sizes.deme .== d]) for d in 1:4]
```

Or the steps of the life cycle can carry parameters, as part of the syntax: `withparams`
gives the steps of a deme's generation a width `ω` or a fixed optimum `θ` of its own,
and `L.migrate(k; rate)` carries its rate (a number or a matrix), so `run_composed` needs
no `migration_rate`:

```{julia}
local_cycle = withparams(g; θ = -0.5) ⊗ withparams(g; θ = 0.5, ω = 0.5) ⋅ L.migrate(2; rate = 0.01)
```

The optimum is a parameter of the step `select`, not of `Params`; the section on local
adaptation below uses it.

## How migration works

The kernel's `migrate!` visits each individual once. With probability `r` it starts an
exchange: it picks a deme (uniformly among the others in the island model, from its row
of the matrix otherwise) and a random individual there, and the two change places. Three
consequences follow.

- Deme sizes are exact. An exchange moves one individual each way, so migration never
  changes a deme's size, as above.
- About twice as many individuals move as start an exchange. A deme's individuals start
  about `N r` exchanges, and as many individuals of the other demes start exchanges with
  it, so the fraction of a deme's adults that came from elsewhere, the backward migration
  rate `m` of population genetics, is about `2r`. `backward_migration(M, N)` computes it
  exactly: a little less than `2r`, because an individual that has moved can be
  exchanged again.
- Exchanges are made one after another, so the order of the demes could matter: with a
  fixed order, deme 1 would send migrants that deme 2 can pass on in the same
  generation, but not the reverse. `migrate!` therefore visits the demes in a new
  uniformly random order at each call, and `randomOrderSweep_exchangeable` in
  `lean/CategoricalQuantGen/Migration.lean` proves that migration is then exchangeable:
  relabelling the demes commutes with it, in distribution, for any migration matrix
  that relabelling leaves unchanged (such as the island model).

The second point can be checked directly. Tag every individual with its deme (in its
environmental-deviation slot, which `migrate!` exchanges with it), migrate once, and
count, 2000 times for each rate, in four demes of 50:

```{julia}
#| output: asis
function migrant_fraction(k, N, r, ncalls, rng)
    s = Params(PopSize = N, Ploidy = 2, Drift = true) ⊗ demes(k)
    f = 0.0
    for _ in 1:ncalls
        for (a, w) in enumerate(s.demes); fill!(view(w.env, 1:w.N), a); end
        migrate!(s, rng; rate = r)
        f += mean(count(!=(a), view(w.env, 1:w.N)) / w.N for (a, w) in enumerate(s.demes))
    end
    f / ncalls
end
println("| rate r | 2r | backward m, exact | measured |\n|--:|--:|--:|--:|")
for r in (0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1)
    m = 1 - backward_migration(4, r, 50)[1, 1]
    @printf("| %g | %g | %.5f | %.5f |\n", r, 2r, m, migrant_fraction(4, 50, r, 2000, Xoshiro(round(Int, 1e4r))))
end
```

So `Nm`, the number of migrants per deme per generation that the classical formulas
take, is $N$ times the backward rate, about $2Nr$; below, every $Nm$ is computed
from `backward_migration`.

## Neutral differentiation

### The model and the statistic

Without selection (`Drift = true`) the trait is neutral, and its differentiation among
demes is a measure of population structure. For an additive trait,
$Q_{ST} = \sigma^2_B / (\sigma^2_B + 2 V_W)$, with $\sigma^2_B$ the variance among deme
means and $V_W$ the additive variance within demes, has the same expectation as
Wright's $F_{ST}$ at neutral loci [@Spitze1993; @Whitlock1999]. Here $\sigma^2_B$ is the
variance among the deme means relative to the whole metapopulation (Wright's convention,
as in @Takahata1983 and @Slatkin1991): $(k-1)/k$ times the variance among the $k$ deme
means, less the sampling variance of a deme mean, $V_W/N$.

The demes have $N = 50$ diploids with 20 loci and a mutational variance
$V_m = 0.001$ per individual per generation. The statistics are on genotypes, which the
standard records do not keep for each deme, so a custom image of the step `record`
collects them at chosen generations. QTLSim's lowering takes images of steps from the
`images` dictionary, so changing what is recorded changes no other step:

```{julia}
p0 = Params(Ploidy = 2, NoQTL = 20, RecombPoissonMean = 1.0, PhenotypeVar = 1.0, Heritability = 0.5,
            MutationScalar = 0.002, MutationRatePerGamete = 0.05, Drift = true)
Vm = muteVar(p0)

"Run `ps ⊗ demes(k)`, recording each deme's mean and variance of genotypes at the census generations."
function census_run(ps, cycle, M, seed, census)
    s = ps ⊗ demes(length(ps))
    idx = IdDict(w => i for (i, w) in enumerate(s.demes))
    mg = zeros(length(ps), length(census)); vg = zeros(length(ps), length(census))
    rec = operator(:record, function (w, rng)
        j = searchsortedfirst(census, w.gen)
        if j <= length(census) && census[j] == w.gen
            gt = view(w.genotype, 1:w.N)
            mg[idx[w], j] = mean(gt); vg[idx[w], j] = var(gt)
        end
        w
    end)
    run_composed(s, Xoshiro(seed); cycle, record = false, images = Dict(:record => rec), migration_rate = M)
    (; mg, vg)
end

"Q_ST from the mean within-deme variance and the mean sample variance among deme means."
qst_of(VW, among, k, N) = (σ2 = (k - 1) / k * (among - VW / N); σ2 / (σ2 + 2VW))
Vm
```

### Theory

`neutral_deme_variances(P, N, Vm)` gives the expected within-deme variance, the variance
among deme means and $Q_{ST}$ exactly, for the kernel's own life cycle, from a recursion
for the expected coalescence times of pairs of genes (`deme_coalescence`), at
equilibrium or at any generation of a run that starts, as the kernel's does, with all
genomes equal [@Slatkin1991; @Whitlock1999]. `P` is the backward migration matrix, and
`origins` the law of the demes two distinct adults came from: `:exchange` is that of the
kernel's exchanges, to first order in the migration rate. For the island model the
equilibrium has a closed form, `qst_island(N, m; k)`, exact when the two adults' origins
are independent (as when migrants are drawn from a common pool):

$$Q_{ST} = \frac{\tfrac{k-1}{k} R}{\tfrac{k-1}{k} R + 1}, \qquad
R = \frac{\lambda}{2N(1 - \lambda)}, \qquad \lambda = \Big(1 - \frac{m k}{k - 1}\Big)^2.$$

For small $m$ it is close to Takahata's $1/(1 + 4Nm\,(k/(k-1))^2)$, and with infinitely
many demes it becomes Wright's $1/(1 + 4Nm)$.

### Simulations

Each scenario runs 50 times for about four times the longest mean coalescence time
(between 1600 and 13,400 generations), and the statistics are averaged over every 10th
generation of the second half of each run. The island model has $k = 4$ and $10$ demes
and $Nm$ from about 0.1 to 10, and the ring has $k = 8$ demes. The predictions are the
exact expectations for the same generations, which are within about 3% of equilibrium
for the variances and closer for $Q_{ST}$.

```{julia}
N = 50; R = 50
plans = []
for k in (4, 10), Nm in (0.1, 0.3, 1.0, 3.0, 10.0)
    push!(plans, (; k, ring = false, M = island_migration(k, Nm / (2N))))
end
for Nm in (1.0, 10.0)
    push!(plans, (; k = 8, ring = true, M = stepping_stone(8, Nm / (2N))))
end
plans = map(plans) do pl
    P = backward_migration(pl.M, N)
    T = maximum(deme_coalescence(P, N; origins = :exchange).S)
    gens = ceil(Int, 4T / 100) * 100
    census = collect(gens ÷ 2:10:gens-1)
    (; pl..., P, m = 1 - P[1, 1], gens, census, p = Params(p0; PopSize = N, NoGenerations = gens),
     cycle = foldl(⊗, fill(g, pl.k)) ⋅ L.migrate(pl.k))
end
jobs = sort!([(i, rep) for i in eachindex(plans) for rep in 1:R]; by = j -> -plans[j[1]].gens * plans[j[1]].k)
runs = Vector{Any}(undef, length(jobs))
elapsed = @elapsed Threads.@threads :greedy for j in eachindex(jobs)
    i, rep = jobs[j]
    pl = plans[i]
    runs[j] = census_run(fill(pl.p, pl.k), pl.cycle, pl.M, 1000i + rep, pl.census)
end
@printf("%d runs in %.0f s on %d threads\n", length(jobs), elapsed, Threads.nthreads())
```

```{julia}
ringdist(a, b, k) = min(mod(a - b, k), mod(b - a, k))
brng = Xoshiro(12)
results = map(eachindex(plans)) do i
    pl = plans[i]; k = pl.k
    rs = [runs[j] for j in eachindex(jobs) if jobs[j][1] == i]
    w = [mean(r.vg) for r in rs]
    a = [mean(var(view(r.mg, :, c)) for c in axes(r.mg, 2)) for r in rs]
    q = qst_of(mean(w), mean(a), k, N)
    boot = sort([(ix = rand(brng, 1:R, R); qst_of(mean(w[ix]), mean(a[ix]), k, N)) for _ in 1:2000])
    th = neutral_deme_variances(pl.P, N, Vm; t = pl.census, origins = :exchange)
    tw, ta = mean(mean(x.within) for x in th), mean(x.among for x in th)
    eq = neutral_deme_variances(pl.P, N, Vm; origins = :exchange)
    # half the squared difference of deme means, by distance on the ring
    dists = pl.ring ? (1:k÷2) : (1:0)
    pairs_sim = [mean(mean((r.mg[x, c] - r.mg[y, c])^2 / 2 for x in 1:k for y in x+1:k if ringdist(x, y, k) == d
                            for c in axes(r.mg, 2)) for r in rs) for d in dists]
    bydist(v, d) = mean(v.pairs[x, y] for x in 1:k for y in x+1:k if ringdist(x, y, k) == d)
    pairs_eq = [bydist(eq, d) for d in dists]
    pairs_pred = [mean(bydist(x, d) for x in th) for d in dists]
    pairs_se = [std([mean(mean((r.mg[x, c] - r.mg[y, c])^2 / 2 for x in 1:k for y in x+1:k if ringdist(x, y, k) == d)
                          for c in axes(r.mg, 2)) for r in rs]) / sqrt(R) for d in dists]
    (; pl.k, pl.ring, pl.m, Nm = N * pl.m, VW = mean(w), VW_se = std(w) / sqrt(R), q, q_lo = boot[50], q_hi = boot[1950],
     q_se = std(boot), q_pred = qst_of(tw, ta, k, N), q_eq = eq.qst, VW_pred = tw, VW_eq = mean(eq.within),
     pairs_sim, pairs_se, pairs_pred, pairs_eq)
end;
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("| demes | Nm | simulated Q_ST (95% CI) | expected at the census | z | exact equilibrium | qst_island | Takahata | Wright |")
println("|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|")
for r in results
    r.ring && continue
    k = r.k
    @printf("| %d | %.3g | %.4f (%.4f–%.4f) | %.4f | %.2f | %.4f | %.4f | %.4f | %.4f |\n", k, r.Nm, r.q, r.q_lo, r.q_hi,
            r.q_pred, (r.q - r.q_pred) / r.q_se, r.q_eq, qst_island(N, r.m; k),
            1 / (1 + 4r.Nm * (k / (k - 1))^2), 1 / (1 + 4r.Nm))
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-qst
#| fig-cap: "Q_ST of a neutral trait among demes of 50 diploids in the island model, against the number of migrants per deme per generation. Points: simulations, 50 runs each, with bootstrap 95% intervals (most are smaller than the points). Solid: the exact equilibrium for the kernel's life cycle (neutral_deme_variances); dashed: Takahata's finite-island approximation; dotted: Wright's 1/(1 + 4Nm)."
fig = Figure(size = (820, 380))
Nms = exp10.(range(-1.1, 1.1, length = 120))
for (col, k) in enumerate((4, 10))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, col], xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xlabel = "Nm (backward)", ylabel = "Q_ST",
              title = "$k demes", xticks = ([0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10], ["0.1", "0.3", "1", "3", "10"]),
              yticks = ([0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1], ["0.01", "0.03", "0.1", "0.3", "1"]))
    island_P(m) = [a == c ? 1 - m : m / (k - 1) for a in 1:k, c in 1:k]
    lines!(ax, Nms, [neutral_deme_variances(island_P(x / N), N, Vm; origins = :exchange).qst for x in Nms],
           color = :black, label = "exact")
    lines!(ax, Nms, [1 / (1 + 4x * (k / (k - 1))^2) for x in Nms], color = :teal, linestyle = :dash,
           label = "Takahata")
    lines!(ax, Nms, [1 / (1 + 4x) for x in Nms], color = :darkorange, linestyle = :dot, label = "Wright")
    rs = filter(r -> r.k == k && !r.ring, results)
    errorbars!(ax, [r.Nm for r in rs], [r.q for r in rs], [r.q - r.q_lo for r in rs], [r.q_hi - r.q for r in rs],
               color = :crimson, whiskerwidth = 6)
    scatter!(ax, [r.Nm for r in rs], [r.q for r in rs], color = :crimson, label = "simulated")
    col == 1 && axislegend(ax, position = :lb)
end
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
zs = [(r.q - r.q_pred) / r.q_se for r in results if !r.ring]
isl = filter(r -> !r.ring, results)
wr(r) = 1 / (1 + 4r.Nm)
worst = argmax(r -> wr(r) / r.q_eq, isl)
best = argmin(r -> wr(r) / r.q_eq, isl)
print(@sprintf("Every simulated Q<sub>ST</sub> agrees with the exact expectation for the generations recorded: the largest of the %d values of |z| is %.2f, ",
               length(zs), maximum(abs, zs)),
      @sprintf("a value that %d comparisons exceed by chance with probability %.2f. ", length(zs),
               1 - (1 - 2cdf(Normal(), -maximum(abs, zs)))^length(zs)),
      @sprintf("Wright's 1/(1 + 4Nm) is furthest off with %d demes and Nm ≈ %.2g, where it gives %.4f against an exact %.4f, %.1f times too much, and closest with %d demes and Nm ≈ %.2g, %.3f against %.3f.\n",
               worst.k, worst.Nm, wr(worst), worst.q_eq, wr(worst) / worst.q_eq, best.k, best.Nm, wr(best), best.q_eq))
```

Wright's formula is the limit of infinitely many demes and rare migration, and it fails
on both counts. With few demes a migrant is more likely to come back to the deme its
ancestors left, which Takahata's factor $(k/(k-1))^2$ accounts for, and the variance
among a few demes, relative to the whole metapopulation, is smaller by $(k-1)/k$. With
much migration the approximations fail too: in four demes, $m k/(k-1) = 1$ is complete
mixing (at $m = 0.75$), and as $m$ approaches it $Q_{ST}$ falls faster than either
approximation predicts. The independent-origins closed form `qst_island` is within a
fraction of a percent of the exact value with exchanges (compare the columns of the
table), too little to see at this number of runs.

### The stepping-stone ring

On a ring of eight demes, demes that are closer are more alike. The pairwise $F_{ST}$
between two demes $d$ steps apart (with $\sigma^2$ half the variance of their two means
and $V_W$ the within-deme variance) is compared with the exact expectation and with
Slatkin's approximation for small $m$, `fst_stepping_stone(N, m, k, d)`
[@Slatkin1991, eq. 17]:

```{julia}
#| output: asis
pair_fst(half_sq, VW) = (σ2 = (half_sq - VW / N) / 2; σ2 / (σ2 + 2VW))
println("| Nm | distance | simulated ½(Ḡa − Ḡb)² | expected at the census | z | pairwise F_ST, simulated | exact equilibrium | Slatkin |")
println("|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|")
for r in filter(r -> r.ring, results), d in 1:r.k÷2
    @printf("| %.3g | %d | %.4f ± %.4f | %.4f | %.2f | %.4f | %.4f | %.4f |\n", r.Nm, d, r.pairs_sim[d], r.pairs_se[d],
            r.pairs_pred[d], (r.pairs_sim[d] - r.pairs_pred[d]) / r.pairs_se[d],
            pair_fst(r.pairs_sim[d], r.VW), pair_fst(r.pairs_eq[d], r.VW_eq), fst_stepping_stone(N, r.m, r.k, d))
end
```

Differentiation rises with distance, as in Kimura and Weiss's stepping-stone model
[@KimuraWeiss1964], and the simulated squared differences follow their exact
expectations for the generations recorded. Slatkin's approximation is a few percent too
high at $Nm \approx 1$ and much too high at $Nm \approx 10$, where $m = 0.2$ is no longer
small.

### The variance within demes, and the exchange

In the textbook island model the expected variance within a deme at equilibrium is
$2NkV_m$, the variance of an undivided population of the same total size, whatever the
migration rate [@Lande1992; @Whitlock1999]. That result assumes that the demes two
adults came from are independent. The kernel's exchanges keep every deme's size exactly,
so two distinct adults of the metapopulation are in the same deme with probability
exactly $(N-1)/(kN-1)$ rather than $1/k$, and the variance within demes becomes

$$V_W = 2NV_m\,\frac{kN - 1}{N - 1},$$

still independent of the migration rate. At $N = 50$ the difference, 1.5% at $k = 4$,
is within the noise of the runs above:

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("| demes | Nm | simulated V_W | expected at the census | 2NkV_m | 2NV_m(kN−1)/(N−1) |\n|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|")
for r in filter(r -> !r.ring, results)
    @printf("| %d | %.3g | %.4f ± %.4f | %.4f | %.4f | %.4f |\n", r.k, r.Nm, r.VW, r.VW_se, r.VW_pred,
            2N * r.k * Vm, 2N * Vm * (r.k * N - 1) / (N - 1))
end
```

The expectations at the census are below both equilibrium values because the runs end
before equilibrium. Most simulated values are a little below their expectations, each
within about two standard errors; `validate/fst.jl`, with eight times as many runs,
finds no discrepancy in the variance within demes (largest $|z|$ 2.6).

In small demes the difference is not negligible. With four demes of $N = 10$, the two formulas differ by 8%;
200 runs of 3000 generations, with $Nm \approx 1$:

```{julia}
#| output: asis
let k = 4, Ns = 10, M = island_migration(4, 0.05), census = collect(1000:10:2990)
    ps = fill(Params(p0; PopSize = Ns, NoGenerations = 3000), k)
    cyc = foldl(⊗, fill(g, k)) ⋅ L.migrate(k)
    w = Vector{Float64}(undef, 200)
    Threads.@threads :greedy for i in 1:200
        w[i] = mean(census_run(ps, cyc, M, 50_000 + i, census).vg)
    end
    P = backward_migration(M, Ns)
    se = std(w) / sqrt(200)
    exch, pool = 2Ns * Vm * (k * Ns - 1) / (Ns - 1), 2Ns * k * Vm
    @printf("Nm = %.2f. Simulated V_W %.5f ± %.5f; 2NV_m(kN−1)/(N−1) = %.5f (z = %.1f); 2NkV_m = %.5f (z = %.1f).\n",
            Ns * (1 - P[1, 1]), mean(w), se, exch, (mean(w) - exch) / se, pool, (mean(w) - pool) / se)
end
```

The simulated variance within demes is the exchange formula's, not the textbook value.
$Q_{ST}$ is hardly affected: the exchange raises the variance among demes in nearly the
same proportion, so that `qst_island`, which assumes independent origins, is within a
fraction of a percent of the exact value, as above. `validate/fst.jl` makes the full
comparison (41 statistics, 400 runs per scenario, with the law of the origins of pairs
measured from `migrate!` itself), and finds no discrepancy (largest $|z|$ 2.6,
`validate/fst.log`).

## Local adaptation

When demes are selected toward different optima, the trait differs among them more than
drift alone would make it, and $Q_{ST} > F_{ST}$ is the classical sign of local
adaptation [@Spitze1993; @Whitlock1999]. Four demes of 50 now select toward optima
$-0.6$, $-0.2$, $0.2$ and $0.6$ (phenotypic standard deviation 1), each through a
`select` step that carries its optimum, with the width $\omega = 1$ from `Params`. The
neutral comparison, standing in for $F_{ST}$ at neutral markers, is the same
metapopulation with every fitness one, and its exact expectation. 20 runs of 3000
generations at each of three migration rates:

```{julia}
#| output: asis
θs = [-0.6, -0.2, 0.2, 0.6]
sel_base = Params(p0; PopSize = N, NoGenerations = 3000, Drift = false, InitFitnessSD = 1.0)
selected = foldl(⊗, [withparams(g; θ) for θ in θs]) ⋅ L.migrate(4)
neutral = foldl(⊗, fill(g, 4)) ⋅ L.migrate(4)
census_la = collect(1500:10:2990)
la_jobs = [(r, kind, rep) for r in (0.002, 0.01, 0.05) for kind in (:selected, :neutral) for rep in 1:20]
la_runs = Vector{Any}(undef, length(la_jobs))
Threads.@threads :greedy for j in eachindex(la_jobs)
    r, kind, rep = la_jobs[j]
    ps = fill(kind === :selected ? sel_base : Params(sel_base; Drift = true), 4)
    la_runs[j] = census_run(ps, kind === :selected ? selected : neutral, island_migration(4, r), 70_000 + j, census_la)
end
println("| Nm | trait | deme means (average) | V_W | Q_ST | neutral expectation |\n|--:|:--|:--|--:|--:|--:|")
for r in (0.002, 0.01, 0.05), kind in (:selected, :neutral)
    rs = [la_runs[j] for j in eachindex(la_jobs) if la_jobs[j][1] == r && la_jobs[j][2] === kind]
    VW = mean(mean(x.vg) for x in rs)
    among = mean(mean(var(view(x.mg, :, c)) for c in axes(x.mg, 2)) for x in rs)
    dm = vec(mean(mean(x.mg; dims = 2) for x in rs))
    P = backward_migration(4, r, N)
    qn = mean(x.qst for x in neutral_deme_variances(P, N, Vm; t = census_la, origins = :exchange))
    @printf("| %.2f | %s | %s | %.3f | %.3f | %.3f |\n", N * (1 - P[1, 1]), kind,
            join((@sprintf("%.2f", x) for x in dm), ", "), VW, qst_of(VW, among, 4, N), qn)
end
```

With rare migration ($Nm \approx 0.2$) drift alone differentiates the demes about as
much as selection does, and the two values of $Q_{ST}$ are close: the selected deme
means sit near their optima, but neutral demes wander as far. As migration increases,
neutral differentiation collapses, while selection keeps the deme means apart, pulled
toward each other by migrants but still in the order of their optima, and $Q_{ST}$ of the
selected trait stays well above the neutral expectation. Selection also lowers the
variance within demes, which raises $Q_{ST}$ further. The neutral runs agree with their
exact expectation, as in the previous section.

## What the moments lowering predicts

The moments lowering ([Recomposing the model](../06_recomposing_the_model/06_recomposing_the_model.qmd))
gives a life cycle its deterministic prediction. With `between = true` it also carries
the expected second moments of genes across demes, so it predicts the variance within
demes, the variance among deme means and $Q_{ST}$ for any life cycle on diploid demes,
with drift, mutation, migration and selection, in the column `metapop`. `origins`
chooses the law of migrants' origins, `:exchange` (the default, the kernel's) or `:pool`.
For a neutral trait it is the exact recursion of `neutral_deme_variances`, generation by
generation; under selection it is an approximation. Below, the four demes of 50 with
$Nm \approx 1$ start, as the kernel's do, with all genomes equal, neutral or selected
toward the four optima of the previous section, and the prediction is set against 30
kernel runs of each, recorded every 20 generations:

```{julia}
#| output: asis
Mla = island_migration(4, 0.01)
traj_census = collect(0:20:2980)
cases = [("neutral", fill(Params(sel_base; Drift = true), 4), neutral),
         ("local optima", fill(sel_base, 4), selected)]
traj_jobs = [(c, rep) for c in eachindex(cases) for rep in 1:30]
traj_runs = Vector{Any}(undef, length(traj_jobs))
Threads.@threads :greedy for j in eachindex(traj_jobs)
    c, rep = traj_jobs[j]
    traj_runs[j] = census_run(cases[c][2], cases[c][3], Mla, 90_000 + j, traj_census)
end
traj = map(eachindex(cases)) do c
    rs = [traj_runs[j] for j in eachindex(traj_jobs) if traj_jobs[j][1] == c]
    VW = [mean(mean(r.vg[:, t]) for r in rs) for t in eachindex(traj_census)]
    among = [mean(var(r.mg[:, t]) for r in rs) for t in eachindex(traj_census)]
    mo = run_moments(cases[c][2]; cycle = cases[c][3], migration_rate = Mla, between = true).metapop
    (; VW, qst = qst_of.(VW, among, 4, N), mo)
end
late = traj_census .>= 1500
println("| trait | V_W, kernel | V_W, moments | Q_ST, kernel | Q_ST, moments |\n|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|")
for (c, tr) in enumerate(traj)
    mlate = tr.mo.gen .>= 1500
    @printf("| %s | %.4f | %.4f | %.4f | %.4f |\n", cases[c][1], mean(tr.VW[late]), mean(tr.mo.within[mlate]),
            mean(tr.qst[late]), mean(tr.mo.qst[mlate]))
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-moments
#| fig-cap: "Four demes of 50 with Nm ≈ 1, starting from equal genomes: the variance within demes (left) and Q_ST (right) over time. Points: 30 kernel runs, from the mean within-deme variance and the mean variance among deme means every 20 generations. Lines: the moments lowering with between = true. Black: a neutral trait; red: demes selected toward optima −0.6, −0.2, 0.2 and 0.6."
fig = Figure(size = (820, 340))
axv = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "variance within demes")
axq = Axis(fig[1, 2], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "Q_ST")
for (c, col) in zip(eachindex(cases), (:black, :crimson))
    tr = traj[c]
    scatter!(axv, traj_census, traj[c].VW, color = (col, 0.5), markersize = 5)
    lines!(axv, tr.mo.gen, tr.mo.within, color = col, label = cases[c][1])
    scatter!(axq, traj_census[2:end], tr.qst[2:end], color = (col, 0.5), markersize = 5)
    lines!(axq, tr.mo.gen[2:end], tr.mo.qst[2:end], color = col)
end
axislegend(axv, position = :rb)
fig
```

For the neutral trait the prediction is exact, and the kernel follows it. With local
optima it captures the main effects: selection holds the variance within demes at less
than half the neutral value and keeps $Q_{ST}$ well above the neutral expectation.
Quantitatively it is a few percent off:

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
let tr = traj[2], ml = tr.mo.gen .>= 1500
    @printf("over generations 1500–2980 its variance within demes is within %.0f%% of the kernel's and it underpredicts Q<sub>ST</sub> by %.0f%%, ",
            max(1, round(Int, 100abs(mean(tr.mo.within[ml]) / mean(tr.VW[late]) - 1))), 100(1 - mean(tr.mo.qst[ml]) / mean(tr.qst[late])))
    println("as `validate/moments_demes.jl` finds under weak selection with five and ten demes: the variance within demes within 4% and Q<sub>ST</sub> 2–7% low (`validate/moments_demes.log`).")
end
```

## Summary

A metapopulation is a product of life cycles followed by migration,
`g ⊗ … ⊗ g ⋅ L.migrate(k)`, run on `p ⊗ demes(k)` by `run_composed`, with the migration
graph a scalar, `island_migration` or `stepping_stone`, and demes given parameters of
their own by a vector of `Params` or by steps that carry them. The kernel's migration
exchanges individuals, so deme sizes never change, about twice as many individuals move
as start an exchange, and the random order in which the demes are visited makes it
exchangeable, which Lean proves. Neutral differentiation in the simulations matches the
exact theory for the kernel's life cycle, in island models of four and ten demes from
$Nm \approx 0.1$ to 10 and on a stepping-stone ring. Wright's $1/(1+4Nm)$ overestimates
$Q_{ST}$ with few demes or much migration, and the exchange raises the variance within
demes above the textbook $2NkV_m$, by a factor $(kN-1)/(k(N-1))$ that matters only in
small demes. The moments lowering with `between = true` predicts the same quantities
deterministically: exactly for a neutral trait, and within several percent under
selection.
